li.a: Texas Tribune: Uvalde school shooting response was a failure, says DOJ
CBS News: DOJ Uvalde report says law enforcement response to school shooting was a failure

content.p: On 24 May 2022 an 18-year-old gunman, Salvador Ramos, killed 19 children and two teachers at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas. Nearly 400 officers from federal, state and local agencies came to the school, yet 77 minutes passed from when law enforcement first arrived to when a tactical team led by the US Border Patrol confronted and killed him. The delay became the central question of the case. Years of official reviews, a grand jury and a criminal trial have followed.

The first prosecution of an officer for the response ended in an acquittal. On 21 January 2026 a jury in Corpus Christi found former school district officer Adrian Gonzales not guilty on all 29 counts. The former school district police chief, Pete Arredondo, has been indicted and awaits his own trial.

The Justice Department's review, published on 18 January 2024, gives the most complete official account of the response. It found that 11 officers from the school district and the Uvalde Police Department reached the school within three minutes of the gunman's arrival and headed towards the classrooms after hearing gunfire. Two of them were hit by shrapnel as the gunman fired, and the group pulled back to take cover. The review found that police did not try the classroom door again for roughly another hour.

The review concluded that from that point officers treated the situation as a "barricaded subject scenario and not as an active shooter situation", even though there were signs that the gunman still posed a threat and that there were victims in the room. Its statement on this point was blunt: "an active shooter with access to victims should never be considered and treated as a barricaded subject", with the word "never" in italics. It called the failure to recognise an active shooter "the most significant failure".

The review also found that many officers who arrived wrongly believed the gunman was dead, or that Arredondo was inside the room with him. Meanwhile, children inside made panicked 911 calls, Al Jazeera reported. The review said that the vast majority of the at least 380 officers had never trained together, which contributed to problems with coordination and communication.

When the room was finally entered, a Border Patrol-led tactical team killed the gunman. Attorney General Merrick Garland said that 33 students and three of their teachers, many of them wounded by gunfire, spent more than an hour in the room with the gunman while officers waited outside.
content.h2: What the federal review blamed on whom
content.p: The 575-page report, the length given by CBS News, was launched in late May 2022 at the request of Uvalde's then mayor, Don McLaughlin. The Office of Community Oriented Policing Services led it with outside experts in emergency management, active shooter response and school safety. Its summary phrase was "cascading failures of leadership, decision-making, tactics, policy and training".

The review named Arredondo, the school district's police chief, as the de facto on-scene commander. It said he "did not provide appropriate leadership, command, and control", including by setting up an incident command structure or directing entry into classrooms 111 and 112. CBS News reported the review's finding that he discarded his radios on arrival, thinking they were unnecessary. The review also said Arredondo turned to evacuating children and teachers from the building, which it called a major contributing factor in the delay: the full evacuation took 43 minutes.

The report did not put the blame on him alone. Houston Public Media quoted it as saying that the leadership of four bodies, the Uvalde Police Department, the school district's police, the county sheriff's office and the state Department of Public Safety, "demonstrated no urgency for establishing a command and control structure." CBS News reported that the review found some failures "may have been influenced by policy and training deficiencies."

Garland said that had agencies followed generally accepted practices and gone straight after the shooter, "lives would have been saved and people would have survived." Associate Attorney General Vanita Gupta called the response "an unimaginable failure". Among the review's recommendations were that all agencies in a region should train together and that officers across the country should receive at least eight hours of active shooter training each year.

The review was almost as critical of what happened after the shooting stopped. It found that children who had been grazed, shot or otherwise hurt received no medical attention and were instead sent on buses to the civic center, which had been set up as a reunification centre. Some families were told wrongly that their relatives had survived, and others learned of deaths from personnel untrained in delivering such news.

The report called the amount of "misinformation, misguided and misleading narratives, leaks, and lack of communication" about 24 May "unprecedented", and said it had harmed the mental health and recovery of families and the wider community. At the news conference, Gupta criticised initial misinformation and conflicting accounts from officials, including Texas Governor Greg Abbott and the Department of Public Safety. The Texas Tribune noted that Abbott had initially praised the response and later said he was misled.

The federal report was not the first official verdict. A July 2022 report from Texas lawmakers described an "atmosphere of chaos" and concluded that law enforcement "failed to prioritize saving the lives of innocent victims over their own safety", according to Al Jazeera. The Texas Tribune counted at least six official probes of the shooting by mid-2024, and said they had largely left victims' relatives frustrated. A city-commissioned review by private investigator Jesse Prado cleared all local officers of wrongdoing, though it noted lapses in leadership. Uvalde Police Chief Daniel Rodriguez announced his resignation days after it became public. Arredondo was fired about three months after the shooting, and about a dozen officers were fired, suspended or retired in the months that followed, the Tribune reported.

Garland told reporters in Uvalde that any decision on charging officers belonged to the local district attorney, not the federal government. District Attorney Christina Mitchell convened a grand jury in January 2024. By 27 June 2024, when the Texas Tribune reported it, the grand jury had indicted Arredondo and Gonzales on felony charges of abandoning or endangering a child, the first criminal charges against law enforcement over the response, the Texas Tribune reported, citing the San Antonio Express-News. Gonzales was charged with 29 counts, one for each of the 19 children who died and the 10 who were wounded and survived.

Legal experts told the Tribune that such cases are hard to prove. The US Supreme Court has held that officers have no constitutional "duty to protect", and prosecutors would have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that the officers had a legal duty to act and that failing to do so caused harm. Jesse Rizo, uncle of Jacklyn Cazares, one of the children killed, said he hoped the indictments were "just the beginning". Local activist Lalo Castillo said he had expected state officials to be charged as well, pointing at state troopers.

Gonzales, then 52, pleaded not guilty. His defence argued he could not receive a fair trial in Uvalde, and the trial was moved to Nueces County, in Corpus Christi, before Judge Sid Harle. Each count carried a maximum of two years in prison. The state called 36 witnesses and the defence called two, KSAT reported.

Prosecutors said Gonzales was among the first officers there and had a unique opportunity to stop the attack after a teaching aide told him where the gunman was. According to ABC News, the aide testified that she repeatedly urged him to act and that he did "nothing". They also argued that he did not follow his training once inside the school. On timing, prosecutors said he waited roughly three and a half minutes before entering the hallway, while the defence said fewer than two minutes passed between his arrival and the gunman entering the fourth-grade classrooms. Special prosecutor Bill Turner told jurors that "the 12 of you will set the bar for law enforcement in these situations". District Attorney Mitchell told them: "We cannot continue to let children die in vain."

The defence said Gonzales never saw the gunman and acted on the limited information he had, gathering information, evacuating children and entering the school. Lead defence attorney Nico LaHood argued the prosecution was singling out one officer for systemic failures: "You can't pick and choose." The defence also pointed out that other officers arrived in the same timeframe and that at least one had a chance to shoot the gunman before he entered the school.

After more than seven hours of deliberation, the jury found Gonzales not guilty on all 29 counts. LaHood said jurors told him they saw "a lot of gaps in the evidence". The case was only the second time in US history that prosecutors had sought to hold a law enforcement officer criminally responsible for a response to a mass shooting; in 2023 a Florida jury had acquitted the former Broward County deputy Scot Peterson after the 2018 Parkland shooting.

Relatives who sat in the courtroom were visibly shaken as the verdict was read. Javier Cazares, whose 9-year-old daughter Jackie was killed, said that the family had "prepared for the worst". Jesse Rizo asked what message the verdict sent: "If you're an officer, you can stand by, stand down, and do nothing while people are executed." Julissa Rizo, Jackie's aunt, rejected the defence's claim that Gonzales had done all he could, saying there had been "two monsters on May 24".

David Shapiro of John Jay College of Criminal Justice, a former prosecutor and FBI agent, told Texas Public Radio that the defence's claim that Gonzales was being scapegoated was probably why he was acquitted. He said he would not be surprised if Arredondo were also acquitted, arguing that a criminal case would have to cover everyone who played a material part in the 77 minutes.

Arredondo, whom investigators have described as the incident commander, has been indicted on child endangerment charges. A San Antonio television station reported on 29 September 2026 that he is awaiting a February trial on the charges. He has not been convicted of anything.

The school itself has stood empty since the shooting and has been kept as evidence, although calls to demolish it began soon after the attack. In September 2026 the board of Uvalde Consolidated Independent School District announced that it would transfer the campus to the City of Uvalde so that a permanent memorial and community park could be built. State lawmakers have set aside $10 million for it, to be stewarded by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department. Board president Jesse Rizo said a committee would guide the process, with the input of victims' families central to deciding what the site becomes. The district has not disclosed the price or when the agreement will be final.
